title: The Gardener of Children: Oberweissbach to Marienthal
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Das Pfarrhaus im Walde: The Motherless Childhood (1782–1796)

stops.name: Oberweissbach, the parsonage of the Thuringian Forest
stops.campa: In the high forest village of Oberweissbach, in the little principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt, Friedrich Wilhelm August Fröbel is born on 21 April 1782, sixth child of the pastor Johann Jacob Fröbel. The parsonage stands under the great church; the father tends five thousand souls scattered over six villages and has little left for the newest one under his roof. The forest breathes around the village. The child who will one day plant gardens for children opens his eyes among firs.
stops.quote: I was born at Oberweissbach, a village in the Thuringian Forest, in the small principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt, on the 21st April, 1782. My father was the principal clergyman, or pastor, there.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827), tr. Michaelis & Moore

stops.name: Oberweissbach, the mother's death
stops.campa: Nine months she nurses him; then Jacobine Eleonore Fröbel, born Hoffmann, fails and dies before her son's first spring. The wound is cut that the whole pedagogy will answer: a lifetime spent restoring to all children the mother-arms he never had. Fröbel himself will name this death the deciding event of his outward life. The infant is handed to servants; the father, buried in his parish and in the building of a new church, withdraws. In the motherless parsonage the seed of the Mutter- und Koselieder is laid.
stops.quote: Soon after my birth my mother's health began to fail, and after nursing me nine months she died. This loss, a hard blow to me, influenced the whole environment and development of my being: I consider that my mother's death decided more or less the external circumstances of my whole life.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Oberweissbach, the walled yard and the strip of sky
stops.campa: A stepmother enters the house and coldness with her; the boy is forbidden the street and confined to the walled yard between church and outbuildings. His whole horizon is the big church in front, the sloping field behind, and above him the clear hill-country sky. Deprived of distance, he learns nearness: the plants of the narrow garden become his first companions, and helping his father at gardening his first office. The sky seen from a walled garden: the child will spend a life giving that sky to other children.
stops.quote: For a long time I remained thus deprived of any distant view: but above me I saw the sky, clear and bright as we so often find it in the hill country; and around me I felt the pure fresh breeze stirring.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Oberweissbach, the hazel buds open the temple
stops.campa: The boy, troubled beyond his years by the sermons' talk of the flesh, is shown by his eldest brother the purple threads of the hazel buds and told that the flowers too are wedded, that sex runs quietly through all creation. The oppression lifts at once. Humanity and nature, soul-life and flower-life, knit together in him in that instant and never again come apart. He receives here, at nine years old, the clue of Ariadne he will follow through the labyrinth: the plant as the mirror of the human being.
stops.quote: I can still see my hazel buds, like angels, opening for me the great God's temple of Nature.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Stadtilm, the uncle's rescue
stops.campa: Superintendent Hoffmann, the dead mother's gentle brother, visits the parsonage, sees what the household is doing to the boy, and writes asking for him entirely. Towards the end of 1792 Friedrich comes to Stadtilm in the wide valley of the Ilm. Where the father's house held severity, mistrust and walls, the uncle's holds mildness, trust and liberty: forty schoolfellows, gardens open to him, the whole valley his playground. He drinks life in long draughts and gains freedom of soul and strength of body: the first proof, lived in his own skin, that kindness educates.
stops.quote: In my father's house severity reigned supreme; here, on the contrary, mildness and kindness held sway. There I encountered mistrust; here I was trusted. There I was under restraint; here I had liberty.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

segments.name: Wald und Pflanze: The Forest as First Teacher (1797–1804)

stops.name: Neuhaus am Rennweg, apprentice to the forester
stops.campa: On Midsummer Day 1797, fifteen and a half years old, Fröbel is bound apprentice to a forester and land-surveyor two days' journey from home. The master, busy with timber-floating, leaves the boy alone in the forest house for weeks, and the forest itself takes over the teaching. He maps the neighbourhood, borrows botany books from a doctor in the little town, collects and dries plants with the greatest care, and walks home from the strolling players' theatre under the stars, fixing moral resolutions in his mind. His church religion quietly becomes a religion of the woods.
stops.quote: My religious church life now changed to a religious communion with Nature, and in the last half-year I lived entirely amongst and with my plants, which drew me towards them with fascination.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)
suggested_refs: Thuringian Forest near Neuhaus am Rennweg

stops.name: Jena, the university of the plant
stops.campa: Carrying money to his student brother in Jena, the seventeen-year-old sees the university city in its high noon, the Jena of Fichte and Schelling, of the young Romantics, and refuses to leave. A small maternal inheritance is unlocked; he matriculates. He hears mathematics, mineralogy, botany, natural history, forest-culture, chemistry, house-building; the air itself carries the doctrine that nature is one living whole. What the forest taught him wordlessly, Jena begins to say aloud: one law unfolds through stone, plant and man.
suggested_refs: University of Jena, collegium building c. 1800

stops.name: Jena, the botanical garden: the plant unfolding
stops.campa: In Batsch's lecture-room and the ducal botanical garden Fröbel watches the plant do openly what the child does in secret: unfold from within, by inner law, needing not to be made but only tended. The lectures on natural history give him for the first time the image of interconnection: each organism a member of one developing whole. Here the master-metaphor of his life takes root: the educator as gardener, the school as garden, the child as a growing plant whose law must be obeyed, not overridden. The word Kindergarten lies forty years ahead, already germinating.
stops.quote: An intimate communion with Nature for more than thirty years... has taught me that plants, especially trees, are a mirror, or rather a symbol, of human life in its highest spiritual relations.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)
suggested_refs: A. J. G. C. Batsch portrait

stops.name: Jena, nine weeks in the university prison
stops.campa: Thirty thalers owed to an eating-house keeper, a father who refuses to pay, a stepmother who inflames him, a trustee who hides behind the letter of the law; and the student is locked nine weeks in the Karzer of Jena. He does not waste the cell: he grinds at Latin grammar, reads Winckelmann's letters, and keeps his inner life alight. Freedom comes only when he formally renounces, before the university board, all claim on his father's inheritance. He walks out disinherited and unbowed: the first of many times the world will make him pay for being Fröbel.
stops.quote: I served as scapegoat to the caprices of the obstinate couple, and languished as such nine weeks long in the university prison at Jena.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Oberweissbach, the father's death
stops.campa: Called home from his first small forestry post, Fröbel keeps the last months of watch at the bedside of the stern pastor who never understood him. In 1802 Johann Jacob Fröbel dies, and the parsonage that was never a home closes behind the son forever. Twenty years old, orphaned twice over, he is now wholly unhoused, and therefore wholly free. The wander-years begin: surveyor, actuary, secretary, a man carrying an unnamed calling from post to post like sealed orders he has not yet been permitted to open.

stops.name: Bamberg, land-surveyor in the secularised bishopric
stops.campa: Early in the spring of 1803 he goes to Bamberg, guessing rightly that the political redrawing of the old episcopal lands will need surveyors. He is taken on at once, maps the town and its district, and holds for a time a government clerkship. The work is measurement: chains, angles, the reduction of living land to line and number. It teaches him exactness while starving his soul. In the evenings he reads Novalis and asks the question that will not be quiet: what is a man for? The compass in his hand keeps pointing somewhere the maps do not show.

stops.name: Gross-Milchow, private secretary in Mecklenburg
stops.campa: The wander-years carry him far north, to the flat raw country of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, as private secretary on the estate of Gross-Milchow. Accounts, letters, the administration of another man's land: the outer life orderly, the inner life burning. Here he resolves at last to make something of himself by a settled profession, and fixes on architecture: the building of forms by law. He does not yet know that the resolve is a cipher, and that the building he is being sent to raise is made of children. From Gross-Milchow the road runs to Frankfurt.

segments.name: Der Ruf: The Calling at Frankfurt and the Flame of Yverdon (1805–1810)

stops.name: Frankfurt, Gruner's Musterschule: the calling strikes
stops.campa: In the early summer of 1805 Fröbel enters Frankfurt to train as an architect, and a friend introduces him to Anton Gruner, headmaster of the new Model School. Fröbel speaks openly of his life and its object, and Gruner, reading him at a glance, pronounces the sentence that turns the hinge of the century's pedagogy. Days later the omen seals it: his testimonials, the architect's credentials, the Jena certificates, are lost in transit, no one ever learns how. Fröbel reads it plainly: Providence itself has torn up the old papers. He accepts the teacher's place. The architect is dead; the educator is born.
stops.quote: 'Oh,' said Gruner, turning to me, 'give up architecture; it is not your vocation at all. Become a teacher. We want a teacher in our own school. Say you agree, and the place shall be yours.'
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Frankfurt, the first lesson: the fish in the water
stops.campa: He stands for the first time before a class, thirty or forty boys of nine to eleven, to teach arithmetic, drawing, geography, German. And the thing happens that happens to the called: the room closes around him like a native element. That same week he writes to his brother that he has found what he never knew yet always missed. Every wandering year, every survey chain and account book, is redeemed in a single hour. From this classroom he never really departs; everything afterwards is its enlargement downward, toward younger and younger children, until it reaches the cradle.
stops.quote: It seemed as if I had found something I had never known, but always longed for, always missed, as if my life had at last discovered its native element. I felt as happy as the fish in the water, the bird in the air.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827); letter to his brother, 1805

stops.name: Yverdon, the first pilgrimage to Pestalozzi
stops.campa: Towards the end of August 1805, before he has taught a full month, Gruner's new master is already on the road to Yverdon, where Pestalozzi has lately raised his standard in the lakeside castle. Received kindly, turned loose in the classrooms, the inexperienced pilgrim watches for a fortnight and comes away shaken and kindled at once: elevated and depressed, aroused and bewildered. He senses that heart and mind would come to grief if he stayed longer now; he is not yet strong enough for this fire. He carries the teaching-plan home like an ember wrapped in cloth.
stops.quote: What I saw was to me at once elevating and depressing, arousing and also bewildering.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Frankfurt, return with the ember
stops.campa: In mid-October 1805 he is back at the Model School with his definite appointment from the Consistorium and a settled vow to return to Yverdon for a longer stay. He throws himself into the reorganisation of the whole school upon Pestalozzian lines, teaching by the new method, testing it against thirty living boys at a time. Two years he serves here, the Swiss flame banked in a Frankfurt stove. When consulted on matters he has never studied, he looks within and to Nature for the answer, and the answer gladdens the inquirer.
stops.quote: I left Yverdon in mid-October (1805) with a settled resolution to return thither as soon as possible for a longer stay.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Frankfurt, the Holzhausen Oede: tutor of three boys
stops.campa: Caroline von Holzhausen gives him her three sons entire, and Fröbel leaves the school to become their tutor, moving with the boys out to the family's garden estate, the Oede, before the gates of the city. Here he makes his first whole experiment: education not by lessons alone but by a shared life: garden work, walks, the day itself as teacher. He learns what a family is from inside one, he the motherless man in a mother's household; and he learns that his three pupils are not enough school for him. All four of them must go to Pestalozzi.

stops.name: Yverdon, arrival with the three pupils
stops.campa: In 1808 tutor and pupils travel together to Yverdon and settle in the shadow of the castle, lodging at its very gates when the castle itself is refused them, to live for two years inside Pestalozzi's experiment as scholars among the scholars. Fröbel comes expecting everything; he takes the boys to the common meals, the common lessons, the whole common life. He has arrived at the master's side at the flood-tide of the institute, and he means to receive the flame whole: not the methods only, but the love beneath the methods.
stops.quote: With such expectations I arrived at Yverdon. There was no educational problem whose resolution I did not firmly expect to find there.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Yverdon, the master's flame: evenings on the lake shore
stops.campa: A year deep in the work, Fröbel walks each evening from the schoolrooms to the hills and the shore of Lake Neuchâtel, and the walks become liturgy: sunset on the glaciers, the pine forests bathed in rosy light, Pestalozzi's evening addresses on noble manhood still sounding in him. Nature herself, unsought, draws the walkers close. Here he first thinks systematically of his brother's children in Thuringia, and begins extracting and classifying everything at Yverdon that a family could use: the Keilhau institute drafted, unknowingly, on the shore of a Swiss lake.
stops.quote: As I wandered on the sunlit, far-stretching hills, or along the still shore of the lake, clear as crystal, smooth as a mirror, or in the shady groves, under the tall forest trees, my spirit grew full with ideas of the truly god-like nature and priceless value of a man's soul.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Yverdon, farewell to Pestalozzi
stops.campa: In 1810 the discipleship completes itself the only way true discipleship can: by departure. Fröbel has seen the glory of the institute and also its wound: the want of inner unity, of organic ground-principle beneath the methods; all that is good and all that is imperfect at Yverdon have alike become his teachers. He takes his pupils home by Bern, Schaffhausen and Stuttgart, resolved to equip himself at a German university with the natural science an educator must have. He carries the master's flame away in a vessel the master never possessed: the idea of law-governed development.
stops.quote: On the whole I passed a glorious time at Yverdon, elevated in tone, and critically decisive for my after life.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

segments.name: Kristall und Schwert: The Crystal and the Sword (1811–1815)

stops.name: Göttingen, languages, sciences, and the law of the sphere
stops.campa: At Göttingen the returned disciple sets out to read the universe from both ends: ancient languages to reach the childhood of mankind, natural sciences to reach the law of its growth. In solitary walks he arrives at his great simplification: one law of development running unbroken from stone through plant to the human soul, the spherical law in which every particular unfolds the whole. What he traced at Göttingen amid outward circumstances, confirming the order of the soul's development, he will soon find written a hundredfold in stone. Chemistry and physics point him onward: to Berlin, to the crystals.

stops.name: Berlin, crystallography under Weiss
stops.campa: In October 1812 Fröbel comes to Berlin to sit under Christian Samuel Weiss, the great crystallographer. The lectures he has longed for answer him exactly: in the fixed forms of crystals he sees demonstrated the inner connection of the whole cosmical development of the universe: diversity forever unfolding within unity. The crystal is the child's future Gifts prefigured in stone: sphere, cube, law-formed unfolding. To hold himself at the university he teaches in a Berlin school, and finds he can now turn his thoughts once more to educational problems, armed.
stops.quote: The lectures for which I had so longed really came up to the needs of my mind and soul, and awakened in me, more fervent than ever, the certainty of the demonstrable inner connection of the whole cosmical development of the universe.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Berlin, the call to arms: the teacher's reason for war
stops.campa: The fateful year 1813 opens; all Prussia grasps weapons against Napoleon. Fröbel is no Prussian and owns, he says, a Motherland rather than a Fatherland; yet he enlists, and for a reason no soldier ever gave before him: every child he might one day educate will have a Fatherland, and the man who declined to defend it with his blood could never stand unashamed before a child again. His enthusiasm is small, his determination fixed as rock. It is the first article of the pedagogy, written before the pedagogy: the teacher must be whole before the children.
stops.quote: Every boy, that every child, who might perhaps later on come to be educated by me would have a Fatherland, that this Fatherland was now requiring defence, and that the child was not in a position to share in that defence.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Dresden, Eastertide muster of the Lützowers
stops.campa: At Eastertide 1813 Fröbel reaches Dresden on his way to the black-uniformed infantry of Lützow's Free Corps. Among the crowds of vigorous volunteers, many of them Berlin students like himself, the self-concentrated scholar knows not one man. He has chosen the Lützowers because they fight for no single crown but for a pure German brotherhood, the ideal he has honoured in his soul as lofty and sublime. The weak-bodied naturalist shoulders a musket among strangers, trusting the campaign to furnish what his whole life has lacked: brothers.
stops.quote: As comrades I selected the Luetzowers; and at Eastertide 1813 I arrived at Dresden on my road to join the infantry division of Luetzow's corps.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)
suggested_refs: Black uniform of the Lützow volunteers

stops.name: Meissen, the Elbe evening: Langethal and Middendorff found
stops.campa: First day's march, first halt: at Meissen, on a lovely spring evening, the corps' students gather by the Elbe over old Meissen wine, twenty strong at a long table, pledging friendship. A sergeant has already introduced Fröbel to a fellow Thuringian: Langethal; and here at the table Langethal presents his Berlin friend, the young divinity student Middendorff. Next morning the three visit the cathedral together. The lifelong brothers are found in the first bivouac of the war: Keilhau, Kindergarten, the whole gardened future, is seated at that table without knowing its own name.
stops.quote: Thus from the very first did we three join fast in a common struggle towards and on behalf of the higher life.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Havelberg, the armistice camp: Bauer closes the circle
stops.campa: Through the summer armistice the corps lies in quarters by the Havel, and camp-life does its quiet work: at Havelberg Fröbel strikes up with Bauer, the third friend of Langethal and Middendorff, and the narrow circle of his companions-in-arms is closed. Four students under arms, talking education between drills: the corps marches, skirmishes, endures the campaign into the Netherlands, and the friendship endures with it. He will say the war gave him no wounds and four brothers; the Fatherland he fought for turns out to be a schoolhouse not yet built.
stops.quote: It was more particularly at Havelberg, later on, that Bauer and I struck up a friendship together, which has ever since endured.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Berlin, the mineralogical museum: the godlike in the very small
stops.campa: The war done, Weiss calls his student back as assistant at the royal mineralogical museum. Alone in the locked, perfectly quiet room, ordering stones of the most minute dimensions, Fröbel receives the revelation of his middle life: even in these torn fragments of rock lie germs of developing energy; under all modifications, one law of development. The crystals become a mirror in which he descries mankind. Sweden offers him a professorship of mineralogy; he refuses it. A man to whom stones preach children cannot spend his life cataloguing stones.
stops.quote: I saw clearly, as never yet I had seen before, that the godlike is not alone in the great; for the godlike is also in the very small... And thereafter my rocks and crystals served me as a mirror wherein I might descry mankind, and man's development and history.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

segments.name: Keilhau: The Institute on the Hillside (1816–1830)

stops.name: Griesheim an der Ilm, the Universal German Educational Institute
stops.campa: He resigns the museum, refuses the Stockholm chair, and walks out of Berlin with almost nothing, telling no one his aim. In the village of Griesheim on the Ilm, where his dead brother Christoph was minister, the widow gives him Christoph's three orphaned sons; his brother in Osterode sends two more. With five nephews in a village room, on 16 November 1816, Fröbel opens the Universal German Educational Institute: the whole reform of German education begun as one uncle keeping school for his brothers' children. He writes to Middendorff at Berlin: come, and bring Langethal.
stops.quote: I reckon, therefore, the duration of my present educational work from November 16th, 1816.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Keilhau, the move to the hillside
stops.campa: Middendorff has come in April, straight from Berlin, the first brother to answer; in June 1817 the little school moves to Keilhau, a hamlet folded into the hills by Rudolstadt, and takes root for good. Langethal arrives in September; a frame schoolhouse rises by November on ground Fröbel does not yet own. Poverty is the daily bread, but on this hillside the war-brothers convert their bivouac covenant into an educating household: gardens, wanderings, work, German dress, the child unfolded like the plant. Keilhau becomes the mother-house of everything that follows.
stops.quote: In June of the same year (1817) family reasons caused me to move from Griesheim to this place, Keilhau.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)
suggested_refs: Keilhau institute buildings under the Kirschberg

stops.name: Berlin, marriage to Wilhelmine Hoffmeister
stops.campa: On 11 September 1818, in Berlin, Fröbel marries Henriette Wilhelmine Hoffmeister, a war-councillor's daughter of cultivated mind who has heard the idea in the man and chooses it with open eyes. She leaves the capital for a debt-ridden hamlet in the Thuringian hills, brings her fortune to the hungry institute, and becomes the first mother of the motherless man's great household. For twenty-one years she will carry Keilhau, Switzerland and Blankenburg beside him. The community calls the marriage what it is: the institute's own hearth being lit.

stops.name: Keilhau, growth, suspicion, and the inspector's verdict
stops.campa: The institute swells to some sixty pupils; the boys wear open collars and long hair, climb, garden, wander, and are educated by life itself, and reaction smells sedition in it. In the demagogue-hunting years Keilhau is denounced as a nest of revolution, and Prussia sends the inspector Zeh to examine it. He finds no conspiracy: he finds a wonderfully united family of sixty, living education instead of enduring it, and says so in his report. The verdict acquits, yet frightened parents withdraw their sons; the institute survives on faith and debt, as it always has.

stops.name: Keilhau, 'Die Menschenerziehung': the book of the eternal law
stops.campa: In 1826, out of the hillside's daily practice, Fröbel publishes The Education of Man, and opens it with a sentence that is the whole doctrine in miniature: an eternal law lives and works in all things. Education is named as leading man to a free representation of that inner law: not pouring in, but unfolding; the gardener's book written by the crystallographer. The weekly journal of the community carries on its masthead the six words that will one day stand on his gravestone: Come, let us live for our children.
stops.quote: In all things there lives and works an eternal law... This all-controlling law is necessarily based on an all-pervading, energetic, living, self-conscious, and hence eternal Unity... This Unity is God.
stops.quote_source: Die Menschenerziehung / The Education of Man (1826), tr. W. N. Hailmann, opening

stops.name: Helba, the national plan that heaven deferred
stops.campa: The Duke of Meiningen, won by the long autobiographical letter Fröbel has addressed to him, offers the estate of Helba for a great public educational institution: the Keilhau idea raised to the scale of a nation, with workshops, gardens and school as one organism. Plans are drawn, hopes rise high; then court intrigue and cautious counsellors strangle the scheme in the cradle by 1829. Fröbel walks away from the wreck carrying the plan's deepest layer intact: the conviction that the reform must begin further down, below the school, in earliest childhood.
suggested_refs: Schloss and estate of Helba near Meiningen

segments.name: Die Schweizer Jahre: The Swiss Exile (1831–1836)

stops.name: Schloss Wartensee, the castle on Lake Sempach
stops.campa: Invited by the composer Xavier Schnyder von Wartensee, Fröbel crosses into Switzerland in 1831 and opens an institute in the little castle above Lake Sempach. The liberal cantons hunger for the new education; the clergy of Lucerne scent heresy in the Protestant German and preach against him from the parishes. The school in the castle stays small under the pressure, but the seed shows its vigour: the townsmen of Willisau, having seen the work, petition to have it, priests notwithstanding. Exile, as always with Fröbel, is expansion wearing the mask of defeat.

stops.name: Willisau, the school in the teeth of the priests
stops.campa: At Willisau the townspeople give the Keilhau men a public institute, and it flourishes against a rising wall of clerical fury: sermons against the German educators, threats, the school made a battlefield of the cantonal war between old faith and new light. A public examination is held; the parents see their children and are won; enrollment climbs even as the pulpits thunder. Fröbel, twice denounced now, as demagogue in Prussia, as heretic in Lucerne, learns to read persecution as the shadow every real light casts.

stops.name: Burgdorf, the orphanage: Pestalozzi's own ground
stops.campa: The government of Bern calls Fröbel to direct the cantonal orphanage at Burgdorf: the very town where Pestalozzi began. The circle closes: the disciple keeps school on the master's first ground. Charged also with refresher courses for the canton's teachers, he watches the youngest orphans and the village children and the conviction ripens to certainty: all schooling comes too late; the decisive education happens before the sixth year, in play, at the mother's knee. In the orphan-house of Burgdorf, he who was half an orphan, the kindergarten becomes inevitable.

stops.name: Burgdorf, New Year 1836: 'Renewal of Life'
stops.campa: At the turn of the year the vision arrives whole, and Fröbel writes it down under a title that is itself a proclamation: the year 1836 demands a renewal of life. The renewal of a people, he sees, cannot be legislated or preached; it must be grown, and it begins in the nursing of earliest childhood: a new institution, neither school nor asylum, where the smallest children unfold through play as plants in a tended garden. The thing now exists entire in the spirit. Only the body, the town, and the name remain to be found.
stops.quote: Erneuung des Lebens erfordert das neue Jahr 1836. (The new year 1836 demands a renewal of life.)
stops.quote_source: Title of Fröbel's manuscript essay, Burgdorf, 1836
suggested_refs: Manuscript 'Erneuung des Lebens erfordert das neue Jahr 1836'

stops.name: Burgdorf, departure: the sick wife, the homeward road
stops.campa: Wilhelmine's health breaks in the sharp mountain air, and the physicians order her away from Switzerland. Fröbel resigns his post; Langethal and Ferdinand Fröbel keep Burgdorf, Middendorff turns home to Keilhau. Husband and wife travel to Berlin to settle her inheritance, and in the capital's nurseries and infant-schools Fröbel studies what exists for small children and finds it dead: minding without unfolding. The idea conceived at Burgdorf hardens on the journey into resolve. He returns to the Thuringian hills carrying the kindergarten like a child coming to term.
suggested_refs: Road from Burgdorf toward Bern, 19th-century view

segments.name: Der Kindergarten: The Garden of Children (1837–1848)

stops.name: Bad Blankenburg, the Haus über dem Keller: the first institution for small children
stops.campa: In 1837, in the little town of Blankenburg an hour's walk over the hills from Keilhau, Fröbel rents an old powder-mill house called 'über dem Keller' and opens his Institution for the Fostering of the Activity Impulse of Childhood and Youth: the first house on earth built around the play of small children. Balls, blocks, songs, ring-games in the garden: the fifty-five-year-old man sits on the floor among three-year-olds, and those who watch understand nothing yet. The institution has everything except its true name, which is still walking toward him.
stops.quote: Play is the purest, most spiritual activity of man at this stage... It gives, therefore, joy, freedom, contentment, inner and outer rest, peace with the world.
stops.quote_source: The Education of Man (1826), tr. W. N. Hailmann, the doctrine enacted at Blankenburg
suggested_refs: Fröbel museum 'Haus über dem Keller', Bad Blankenburg

stops.name: Bad Blankenburg, the Gifts, and the Sunday paper of the children
stops.campa: The crystallographer's revelation becomes a toy: the soft ball first, then sphere, cylinder and cube, then the divided blocks: the Spielgaben, play-Gifts, each one the eternal law of unfolding placed into a child's hands. Fröbel and his helpers make them, box them, and carry them like colporteurs of a new scripture; from 1838 his Sonntagsblatt spreads the play-theory under the motto that is his whole confession: Come, let us live for our children. Toy-merchants shrug; mothers begin, slowly, to understand. The Gifts go out from Blankenburg into the world's nurseries.
stops.quote: Kommt, lasst uns unsern Kindern leben!
stops.quote_source: Motto of Fröbel's Sonntagsblatt (1838)
suggested_refs: The Second Gift: sphere, cylinder, cube

stops.name: Dresden, carrying the Gifts to the cities
stops.campa: Fröbel takes the new education on the road: Dresden, Leipzig, Frankfurt, Göttingen, lecturing on play and the Gifts, folding paper before assemblies of skeptical schoolmen and attentive mothers. In Dresden he opens a play-circle and speaks before the court city's educators: the spectacle of an old man demonstrating ball-games as the foundation of national renewal draws mockery and discipleship in equal measure. Every city he leaves keeps a knot of converted women. He has discovered his true army, the one the Prussian ministry will one day fear: mothers.

stops.name: Bad Blankenburg, the death of Wilhelmine
stops.campa: On 13 May 1839 Wilhelmine dies, worn through by twenty-one years of shared poverty and shared faith: the war-councillor's daughter who chose the hillside, whose fortune fed the institute and whose quiet sense steadied its founder. Fröbel walks from her deathbed back to the little ones of Blankenburg; grief in him always converts to work for children. The household of the childless couple had been all children; now the widower gives himself wholly to the youngest, and the last barrier of private life falls away.

stops.name: The Steiger above Blankenburg, the NAME arrives
stops.campa: Spring 1840. Fröbel walks with Middendorff and Barop over the Steiger pass toward Blankenburg, tormented for weeks by the want of a name for his youngest-born institution. On the height, with the town at their feet, he suddenly stops as if fettered to the spot; his eyes take on a strange refulgent brilliancy; and he shouts to the mountains so that it echoes to the four winds. Kindergarten: garden of children. The word is not coined, it is received; the hills of Thuringia are its first witnesses, and the echo has not yet died.
stops.quote: Eureka! I have it! KINDERGARTEN shall be the name of the new Institution!
stops.quote_source: Johannes Barop's reminiscence (c. 1862), in Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel, tr. Michaelis & Moore
suggested_refs: Fröbelblick memorial stone above Bad Blankenburg

stops.name: Bad Blankenburg town hall, founding of the Universal German Kindergarten
stops.campa: On 28 June 1840, amid the four-hundredth jubilee of Gutenberg's press, Fröbel gathers the town in the Blankenburg Rathaus and founds the Allgemeiner Deutscher Kindergarten: deliberately yoking his institution to the printing press as the second great engine of the people's enlightenment. What Gutenberg did for the word, the kindergarten shall do for the child. Shares are subscribed, the women especially called to the work; the play-school 'über dem Keller' becomes the mother-garden of a planted world. From this hall the word Kindergarten begins its unstoppable emigration into every language on earth.

stops.name: Bad Blankenburg, the Mutter- und Koselieder
stops.campa: In 1844 appears the strangest and tenderest of all pedagogical books: the Mutter- und Koselieder, mother-songs, caressing-songs, finger-plays, each with its picture, its melody, its whispered commentary to the mother. Pat-a-cake raised to philosophy: the weather-vane, the fish in the brook, the light-birds on the wall, every game a first lesson in the unity of life. It is the motherless man's letter to the mother he never had, dictated to every mother in Germany. Fröbel holds it the deepest of his books; the world will take a generation to agree.

stops.name: Rudolstadt, the teachers' assembly of the springtime of peoples
stops.campa: The revolutionary spring of 1848 raises every hope at once, and Fröbel's with them: now, surely, the new Germany will found itself upon the new childhood. At the great teachers' assembly in Rudolstadt in August, hundreds of schoolmen debate the people's education; Middendorff, Fröbel's Aaron, his spokesman since the bivouacs, pleads the kindergarten cause, and the assembly resolves that the kindergarten belongs in the free state's order. Petitions go to the Frankfurt parliament. For one bright year the garden of children and the garden of liberty seem to be one garden.

segments.name: Verbot und Abend: The Ban and the Evening at Marienthal (1849–1852)

stops.name: Bad Liebenstein, 'the old fool' and the Baroness
stops.campa: Settled in a farmhouse by the spa of Liebenstein, Fröbel trains young women as kindergartners and dances ring-games in the meadow with the village children. The spa guests are told of 'the old fool' on the hill. In May 1849 the Baroness Bertha von Marenholtz-Bülow follows the phrase to its source, watches the grey-haired man leading his troop of children, and recognizes at sight what the villagers cannot: not a fool but a founder. She becomes the apostle of his cause to courts and salons: the interpreter the slow-tongued prophet has waited for all his life.

stops.name: Hamburg, the winter mission to the free city
stops.campa: Middendorff's eloquence has conquered Hamburg beforehand; in the winter of 1849–50 Fröbel comes in person, called by the women's association of the free city to lead courses for kindergartners at their new Hochschule for the female sex. The halting speaker after the golden-tongued herald disappoints the fashionable and wins the earnest: Wichard Lange, his future editor, attaches himself here. Hamburg's merchants' daughters learn finger-plays and the philosophy of play; the kindergarten takes root in the north. The women of Germany are becoming, parish by parish, the church of his idea.
suggested_refs: Hamburg Hochschule für das weibliche Geschlecht (1850)

stops.name: Marienthal, the duke's gift: the last garden
stops.campa: Won by Marenholtz-Bülow's advocacy, Duke Georg of Saxe-Meiningen gives Fröbel the little hunting-château of Marienthal, between Liebenstein and Schweina, for his training institution. The old man moves in with his kindergartners-in-training, his Gifts, his songs; the meadows become playgrounds, the château a mother-school. Twenty years after Helba fell through, a Meiningen duke at last houses the idea, not the grand national institute of 1829, but its ripened seed: a house where young women learn the tending of childhood. Marienthal, Mary's valley, the gardener's last garden.

stops.name: Marienthal, marriage to Louise Levin
stops.campa: On 9 June 1851 the sixty-nine-year-old Fröbel marries Louise Levin, thirty-six, once a housekeeping pupil at Keilhau, long the most devoted worker of the household. The tongues of the neighbourhood and even of old friends wag; the marriage answers them by simply being what it is: the ordering of the last workshop. Louise stands beside him through the year of the ban, keeps the house of the training school, and after his death will carry his papers, his letters and his cause for half a century of widowhood. The last brotherhood he founds has one member.

stops.name: Marienthal, the Prussian Kindergarten Ban
stops.campa: On 7 August 1851 the Prussian minister von Raumer outlaws the kindergarten throughout Prussia as 'atheistic and demagogic', destructive in religion and politics: the minister has confounded Friedrich with his socialist nephew Karl, whose book on women's colleges and kindergartens frightened the reaction. Varnhagen writes it plainly in his diary: the stupid minister has confused the two Fröbels. The error is exposed; Raumer, rather than admit it, lets the ban stand. The old man at Marienthal, who fought Napoleon for the children of Prussia, sees Prussia close its gardens against the children. The grief never quite leaves him; the ban outlives him by eight years.

stops.name: Marienthal, the seventieth birthday festival
stops.campa: On 21 April 1852 the banned man turns seventy, and Marienthal answers Berlin with flowers. Kindergartners, Keilhau brothers, children of the villages come with garlands and ring-games; the meadows fill with song; the old man is crowned by the small hands his life has served. Middendorff speaks; the children dance the circle-games from the Mutter- und Koselieder around their gardener. Those present remember it afterwards as a transfiguration, the whole doctrine visible for one afternoon: the unity of life, celebrated by playing children in a garden, with the state's prohibition powerless at the fence.

stops.name: Gotha, the teachers rise to greet him
stops.campa: Weeks before the end, Fröbel travels to the general congress of German teachers at Gotha. When the white-haired man enters, the great assembly rises to greet him as one body. The profession that ignored, mocked and suspected him for forty years stands up for the banned founder of the garden of children. Honour arrives, as it likes to, at the door of death. He receives the ovation gently and speaks of the work, not the wound. It is his last journey. He returns to Marienthal carrying the teachers' homage like late fruit, out of season and sweet.

stops.name: Marienthal, death of the gardener
stops.campa: Midsummer 1852: fifty-five years to the season since the boy was bound to the forester on Midsummer Day. On 21 June, at Marienthal, with Louise and the faithful about him and the windows open to the green he loved, Friedrich Fröbel dies. He goes out at the year's greatest light, asking that his flowers be tended and grieving nothing but the closed gardens of Prussia. Middendorff, his Aaron, survives him barely a year; the ban survives him eight; the kindergarten survives him everywhere. The unfolding he preached in crystal, plant and child now claims the preacher.

stops.name: Schweina, the grave under the sphere, cylinder and cube
stops.campa: On 24 June 1852 they carry him from Marienthal up to the hillside churchyard of Schweina, children and kindergartners walking in the procession, and lay him in earth within sight of the Thuringian forest that first mothered him. Over the grave the tradition raises his own second Gift monumentally in stone, sphere upon cylinder upon cube, the eternal law of unfolding set as a tombstone, and cuts beneath it the six words of his life. Lilies, his flower, six-petaled like the motto, are planted round. The gardener is himself planted; the gardens keep coming up, in every country, every autumn, ever since.
stops.quote: Kommt, lasst uns unsern Kindern leben!
stops.quote_source: Fröbel's motto (Sonntagsblatt, 1838), inscribed on the gravestone at Schweina
